title: Mae Sot Itinerary 1-3 Days: Border Town, Markets, Burmese Temples & Food
metaDesc: An hour-by-hour Mae Sot itinerary in Tak, on the Thai-Myanmar border: 1 day, 2 days 1 night, or 3 days 2 nights. Walk Rim Moei and Pa Charoen markets, visit Wat Thai Wattanaram, eat Burmese food, and reach Mae Kasa Waterfall, the Blue Cave and Curve 33.

h1:
Mae Sot Itinerary
The Thai-Myanmar Border Town
intro: Mae Sot is the westernmost district of Tak, about 80 km from Tak town. Cross over the Tenasserim hills and you reach the Moei River, which separates Thailand from Myawaddy in Myanmar. What makes this place special is the blend of two cultures — bilingual shop signs, gilded Burmese-style temples, markets selling both Thai and Burmese goods, and food that's hard to find anywhere else. This itinerary is laid out hour by hour so you can actually follow it, with options for 1 day, 2 days 1 night, or 3 days 2 nights.

blocks.html: First, the big picture. Mae Sot is easy to get around because the town is small — the food, temples and markets in town are all close together, reachable on foot or by tuk-tuk. The nature spots like Mae Kasa Waterfall, the Blue Cave and the viewpoints sit outside town, so you'll need a vehicle for those. The plans below start with the in-town days, then expand outward depending on how many days you have. The prices listed are rough ranges and may shift with what you order and the season.

blocks.text: Getting to Mae Sot and where to stay

blocks.html: Mae Sot has direct buses from Bangkok straight to the district, plus flights into Mae Sot Airport, which is more convenient than busing on from Tak town and crossing the hills. For getting around once you're here, renting a motorbike or car is the way to go, since the out-of-town spots have no public transport. Most accommodation is clustered in the district itself — staying near Prasat Withi Road or the market area puts you within walking distance of food and sights.

items: Car / motorbike — essential if you're heading out of town to the waterfalls or viewpoints. Rental shops are in the district.
Cash — many market stalls and small shops take cash only, so keep small notes on hand.
Accommodation — ranges from budget guesthouses to mid-range town hotels. Book ahead in the cool season, when it gets busy.

blocks.title: Border facts to know before you plan
blocks.html: The Thai-Myanmar border situation changes over time. The crossing into Myawaddy may open or close depending on the period, so if you plan to cross over, check the news and ask at the checkpoint in advance. Travel on the Mae Sot side itself goes on as normal.

blocks.text: 1-day plan — markets, temples and food in town

blocks.html: If you only have one day, this plan covers the heart of Mae Sot — markets, temples and food — without rushing. Start the morning at a fresh market and end the evening with a Burmese meal, staying mostly within town.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Markets, temples and food in a single day

items.activity: Walk Pa Charoen morning market, try mohinga and Burmese snacks
items.note: A market where Thais, Burmese, hill-tribe people and Thai-Chinese all shop side by side — the real atmosphere of a border town.

items.activity: Drive to Rim Moei Market by the Moei River at the end of Highway 105
items.note: See the Thai-Myanmar Friendship Bridge, buy dried goods and souvenirs, and browse the jade and gem stalls.

items.activity: Visit Wat Thai Wattanaram for the red-and-gold hall and the replica Mahamuni Buddha
items.note: A century-old Tai Yai temple, the most photogenic spot in Mae Sot. Dress modestly and take off your shoes before entering the hall.

items.activity: Lunch at Mingalarbar — try the tea-leaf salad and Burmese curry
items.note: The most talked-about Burmese restaurant, a good place if it's your first time trying Burmese food.

items.activity: Stop at Wat Mani Phraison to see the Sambuddhe pagoda and hall
items.note: An in-town temple with fewer crowds, nice for taking your time over the details.

items.activity: Break at BORDERLINE café, sip Burmese tea in a craft gallery
items.note: A café serving Burmese food and drinks, with art from ethnic-minority groups and a relaxed feel.

items.activity: Dinner at Charoen Café, chill over grilled jim-jum hotpot with live music
items.note: An easygoing evening spot to close out the day simply.

blocks.text: 2 days 1 night — add Mae Kasa nature

blocks.html: With an extra day, head out of town to the nature around Mae Kasa subdistrict, which has a waterfall, a cave and a viewpoint. Spend the first day in town like the 1-day plan, stay overnight in the district, then head out to nature on day two.

items.activity: Pa Charoen morning market + Rim Moei Market
items.note: Start as in the 1-day plan, grabbing breakfast bites and souvenirs.

items.activity: Wat Thai Wattanaram + Wat Mani Phraison
items.note: Two temples in the Burmese / Tai Yai style.

items.activity: BORDERLINE café + a stroll around town
items.note: Watch life from two cultures share the same streets.

items.activity: Burmese dinner at Mingalarbar, or Prom Aroi
items.note: Prom Aroi has both Thai and Burmese dishes — the slow-braised oop dishes are good to share. Stay overnight in town.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Mae Kasa nature — waterfall and cave

items.activity: Breakfast at View Doi Coffee Home on the hillside, with wide views
items.note: A 360-degree-view coffee shop just before Mae Kasa Waterfall, good for an easy start to the day.

items.activity: Mae Kasa Waterfall, swim in the clear blue water
items.note: A two-tier waterfall with clear water and no entry fee. More water in the rainy season; clearer in the dry season.

items.activity: The Blue Cave, a blue pool near Mae Kasa Waterfall
items.note: A nature spot people photograph a lot — the water gets its blue tint from minerals in the rock.

items.activity: Lunch at a local spot around Mae Kasa
items.note: A break to eat before heading back into town.

items.activity: Head back into town and catch the food spots you missed
items.note: Nong Benz dim sum the next morning, or Pae Ong roti for a sweet to end the day.

items.activity: Walk the in-town evening market, last round of souvenirs
items.note: Before you head home.

blocks.text: 3 days 2 nights — add viewpoints and hill cafés

blocks.html: With three days, you can easily add a scenic drive around the area. The highlight is Curve 33 at Ban Mae Kon Ken — a winding road through cornfields that, seen from up on the rise, looks like three stacked figures — plus hill cafés scattered across the slopes. Do days one and two as in the 2 days 1 night plan, then add a third day like this.

items.activity: Leave town heading for Ban Mae Kon Ken
items.note: The drive climbs the rise through cornfields, cool air in the morning.

items.activity: Curve 33 viewpoint at Ban Mae Kon Ken
items.note: Photograph the winding road that forms a figure three, with green on both sides. Prettiest from late rainy into early cool season.

items.activity: Stop at a hill café along the way, coffee with mountain views
items.note: Several cafés sit on the slopes — pick whichever you like and linger a while.

items.activity: Lunch, then loop back into town
items.note: Pick a spot along the way or head back to eat in the district.

items.activity: Chao Pho Phawo Shrine, pay respects for a safe trip back
items.note: On the Tak-Mae Sot road, a guardian shrine of the area that drivers passing through often stop at.

items.activity: Catch any food and souvenirs you still missed before heading home
items.note: Close the trip with mohinga or a glass of Burmese milk tea.

blocks.text: Food you shouldn't miss in this plan

blocks.html: Food is the reason a lot of people fall for Mae Sot, since real Burmese food is easier to find here than anywhere else in Thailand. We picked the places reviewers mention most often, spaced out so they fit the timing of the plans above.

items.name: Mingalarbar Mae Sot
items.blurb: The most talked-about Burmese restaurant in Mae Sot, serving bold Burmese curries, tea-leaf salad and mixed rice. A good starting point if it's your first time trying Burmese food.

items.name: BORDERLINE Café
items.blurb: A café serving local-style Burmese food and drinks, with a craft and art gallery from ethnic-minority groups that foreign travelers like to sit in. Good for an afternoon break.

items.name: Prom Aroi Mae Sot
items.blurb: A spot with both Thai and Burmese food under one roof. Standouts are the oop prawns and oop pork, local-style braised dishes that are great for groups sharing.

items.name: Mohinga and Burmese eats at Pa Charoen morning market
items.blurb: Stalls in the morning market serve mohinga (a fish-noodle soup eaten at breakfast), Burmese sweets and cheap Burmese milk tea — street food with a genuine border feel.

items.name: Nong Benz Dim Sum
items.blurb: A morning dim sum spot locals queue for — fragrant, well-rounded broth and good shrimp-wonton noodles at easy prices. A solid breakfast before you head out.

items.name: View Doi Coffee Home
items.blurb: A hillside coffee and food spot just before Mae Kasa Waterfall, with a wide 360-degree view. Good for breakfast or a stop on your nature day two.

blocks.title: Pace your eating
blocks.html: Dim sum and mohinga sell well in the morning — go before late morning to get the full spread. Burmese places like Mingalarbar suit lunch or dinner. Don't pile all the food in at once; leave market walks and temple visits in between and you'll stay comfortably full.

blocks.text: When is the best time to visit Mae Sot

blocks.html: The best stretch is the cool season, November to February — pleasant weather, and walking around in the daytime isn't a struggle. The field and hill views from late rainy into early cool season are lush and green. In the rainy season (June–October) Mae Kasa Waterfall has plenty of water but some roads get slippery, and the hot season is scorching at midday — go in the morning and evening and skip the noon sun.

items: Temple etiquette — many Burmese temples are strict on dress: wear sleeves, cover your knees, take off your shoes before entering the hall, and carry a shawl.
Waterfall and cave — check the weather before you go; trails get slippery in the rainy season, so bring non-slip shoes and waterproofing for your gear.
Timing in town — the in-town sights are close together, so allow time to sit and eat and walk the markets without rushing.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Mae Sot?
faq.a: Just the in-town sights take one day and cover Rim Moei Market, Pa Charoen Market, the Burmese temples and the food. If you also want nature like Mae Kasa Waterfall and the Blue Cave, allow 2 days 1 night. And if you want to add the scenic drive to Curve 33 and the hill cafés, you can easily stretch it to 3 days 2 nights.

faq.q: Where should a Mae Sot itinerary start?
faq.a: Start the morning at Pa Charoen morning market or Rim Moei Market before the crowds, then visit Wat Thai Wattanaram in the late morning, followed by a Burmese lunch — the markets and breakfast food are livelier in the morning than in the afternoon.

faq.q: Do you need your own vehicle in Mae Sot?
faq.a: If you're only doing the in-town sights, walking or a tuk-tuk is enough. But to reach Mae Kasa Waterfall, the Blue Cave or Curve 33 outside town, you'll want a car or a rented motorbike, since there's no public transport to those spots.

faq.q: Which Burmese dishes should you try in Mae Sot?
faq.a: Mohinga (a fish-noodle soup eaten at breakfast) in the morning market, and tea-leaf salad (laphet) at Mingalarbar, are the signature Burmese dishes. BORDERLINE café also serves Burmese drinks and food to try in a relaxed setting.

faq.q: What time does Rim Moei Market open, and can you cross into Myanmar?
faq.a: Rim Moei Market opens daily around 08:00–18:00. The crossing into Myawaddy on the Myanmar side opens and closes depending on the border situation, so check the news and ask at the checkpoint before planning to cross over. Travel on the Mae Sot side itself goes on as normal.
